full_judgment:
7. Obviously, in order to remedy the palpable injustice in the law the amendment introduced by the Ordinance No, XXXVI of 1978 requires the worker concerned to send his grievance petition by registered post within fifteen days of the occurrence of the cause of such grievance. Thereafter, the time taken by the postal authority for delivery of the grievance petition will be the responsibility of the postal authority. It will no longer be the responsibility of the worker concerned. The worker concerned will complete his legal obligation by posting his grievance petition by registered post within fifteen days. It is not his responsibility as to when the registered grievance petition reaches his employer. The worker concerned will also enjoy all the presumption that goes with a registered letter. To hold that the worker concerned is still required to send his grievance petition by registered post well ahead of fifteen days so that the registered grievance petition reaches his employer within fifteen days of the cause of action, will make the amendment meaningless. 

 9. Section 25(1)(a) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act uses the word "submit" and requires the grievance petition to be submitted "in writing by registered post." The rebuttable presumption of section 27 of the General Clauses Act will have full force and application. It will be absolutely in order to equate posting of the grievance petition with the service thereof. We rely upon the case of Md Nurul Islam vs Abdul Malek, 38 DLR (AD) 115 in support of our view.
